summary:
GROUND SHIFT is an interactive Earth-observation investigation game that helps players explore land subsidence in Mexico City using a NASA-published NISAR-derived InSAR visualization. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge “Dancing with the SARs,” the project turns satellite radar science into a four-mission investigation.

Players locate areas of strong ground movement, learn how repeat-pass radar interferometry works, distinguish coherent signals from likely residual noise, and investigate how groundwater extraction and compaction of former lakebed sediments can contribute to subsidence.

The game encourages scientific reasoning by helping players separate observations from interpretations and understand the limits of satellite measurements. It is designed to make complex Earth-observation concepts more accessible and engaging. GROUND SHIFT uses an archived published result, not live monitoring or independent processing of raw NISAR data.
details:
What the project does?

GROUND SHIFT is a browser-based interactive science investigation game about land subsidence in Mexico City. It presents a NASA-published NISAR-derived InSAR visualization as an evidence-based case file. Players take the role of an investigator and complete four missions to understand the observed ground movement.

How it works?

Mission 1 — Detect the Movement:

Players explore the published displacement visualization, locate two major areas of reported subsidence and interpret the map while distinguishing observation from inference.

Mission 2 — Decode the Radar:

Players learn the basic principle of repeat-pass radar interferometry through a clearly labelled schematic explanation of radar acquisitions and phase differences. The schematic is educational, not measured NISAR data.

Mission 3 — Signal or Noise?:

Players classify five image patches as coherent signal, likely residual noise or uncertain. This teaches that scientific interpretation requires recognising noise and uncertainty.

Mission 4 — Solve the Mystery:

Players build a causal explanation connecting groundwater extraction, changes in pore pressure and compaction of clay-rich sediments beneath the city. The game distinguishes the measured displacement from the proposed physical explanation.

A scripted science companion called NOVA provides curated explanations about the evidence, radar concepts and measurement limitations. NOVA is not a live generative AI system.

Benefits and intended impact:

The project makes satellite radar science more approachable through interactive learning. It encourages players to explore Earth-observation evidence, understand how radar measurements reveal surface movement, evaluate uncertainty and avoid making claims beyond what the data supports. It can be used as an educational introduction to SAR and InSAR concepts.

Tools and technologies:

The project was developed as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It uses a NASA-published NISAR-derived visualization and is hosted publicly through GitHub Pages. Development involved Visual Studio Code and the Freebuff AI coding agent.

Creativity and design considerations:

The project presents scientific interpretation as a mystery investigation, using a case-file interface, four progressive missions, evidence classification, a causal reasoning activity, a final report and the scripted NOVA science companion. Scientific transparency was an important design consideration: the project identifies schematic material, explains uncertainty and clearly states that the archived visualization is not live monitoring or a building-safety assessment.

Limitations:

GROUND SHIFT uses an archived NASA-published result for a fixed observation period. It does not independently process raw NISAR data, connect to a live satellite feed, provide real-time monitoring or determine the safety of individual buildings.

Other Information:

ChatGPT was used to assist with project planning, scientific explanations, writing and preparation of submission content. Freebuff AI coding agent was used to assist with HTML, CSS and JavaScript implementation and debugging. The project concept, direction, testing and final decisions were guided by the team. NOVA is a curated scripted science companion, not a live generative AI model. The NASA-published visualization was used as scientific source material and was not AI-generated or modified.
